claim: In vertebrates, condensin I and condensin II cooperate to assemble rod-shaped chromosomes during mitosis.
source: In vertebrates, condensin I and condensin II cooperate to assemble rod-shaped chromosomes during mitosis.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: CAP-D3 plays a crucial role in condensin II-mediated assembly of chromosome axes.
source: We find that one of two HEAT subunits, CAP-D3, plays a crucial role in condensin II-mediated assembly of chromosome axes, whereas the other HEAT subunit, CAP-G2, has a very strong negative impact on this process.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from add-back assays showing that deletion of CAP-D3 prevents axis formation.

claim: CAP-G2 has a very strong negative impact on condensin II-mediated chromosome axis assembly.
source: We find that one of two HEAT subunits, CAP-D3, plays a crucial role in condensin II-mediated assembly of chromosome axes, whereas the other HEAT subunit, CAP-G2, has a very strong negative impact on this process.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that deletion of CAP-G2 greatly increases chromosome association of condensin II.

claim: The structural maintenance of chromosomes ATPase is essential for condensin II-mediated chromosome assembly.
source: The structural maintenance of chromosomes ATPase and the basic amino acid clusters of the kleisin subunit CAP-H2 are essential for this process.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that SMC ATPase mutations prevent chromosome assembly.

claim: The basic amino acid clusters of the kleisin subunit CAP-H2 are essential for condensin II-mediated chromosome assembly.
source: The structural maintenance of chromosomes ATPase and the basic amino acid clusters of the kleisin subunit CAP-H2 are essential for this process.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that mutations in the basic clusters prevent chromosome assembly.

claim: Deletion of the C-terminal tail of CAP-D3 increases the ability of condensin II to assemble chromosomes.
source: Deletion of the C-terminal tail of CAP-D3 increases the ability of condensin II to assemble chromosomes and further exposes a hidden function of CAP-G2 in the lateral compaction of chromosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased chromosome association and altered chromosome morphology with CAP-D3 C-tail deletion.

claim: Deletion of the CAP-D3 C-terminal tail exposes a hidden function of CAP-G2 in the lateral compaction of chromosomes.
source: Deletion of the C-terminal tail of CAP-D3 increases the ability of condensin II to assemble chromosomes and further exposes a hidden function of CAP-G2 in the lateral compaction of chromosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing chromosome morphology between holo(D3-dC) and ΔG2(D3-dC).

claim: Condensin I is localized to the cytoplasm before the onset of mitosis.
source: Before the onset of mitosis, condensin I is localized to the cytoplasm, whereas condensin II is primarily nuclear (Hirota et al., 2004; Ono et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Condensin II is primarily nuclear before the onset of mitosis.
source: Before the onset of mitosis, condensin I is localized to the cytoplasm, whereas condensin II is primarily nuclear (Hirota et al., 2004; Ono et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Condensin II initiates structural changes of chromosomes within the prophase nucleus.
source: This spatial separation allows condensin II to initiate structural changes of chromosomes within the prophase nucleus.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the spatial separation of condensins I and II before mitosis.

claim: After nuclear envelope breakdown, condensin I gains access to the chromosomes and completes the formation of rod-shaped structures.
source: After nuclear envelope breakdown, condensin I gains access to the chromosomes and completes the formation of rod-shaped structures.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about condensin I function during mitosis.

claim: Condensin II contributes to axial shortening, which is followed by lateral compaction mediated by condensin I.
source: Evidence has been provided that condensin II contributes to axial shortening, which is followed by lateral compaction mediated by condensin I (Green et al., 2012; Shintomi and Hirano, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Condensin II plays a more important role in chromosome mechanics than condensin I.
source: As judged by an in situ reorganization assay (Ono et al., 2017) and a mechanical stretching assay (Sun et al., 2018), condensin II plays a more important role in chromosome mechanics than condensin I.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies using specific assays.

claim: Condensin II forms large DNA loops, which are in turn subdivided by condensin I into smaller, nested DNA loops.
source: An emerging model from high-throughput chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C) and quantitative imaging suggests that condensin II forms large DNA loops, which are in turn subdivided by condensin I into smaller, nested DNA loops (Gibcus et al., 2018; Walther et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hi-C and imaging studies.

claim: Condensin I is essential for mitotic chromosome assembly and segregation in all eukaryotic species examined to date.
source: Condensin I is essential for mitotic chromosome assembly and segregation in all eukaryotic species examined to date.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from multiple studies across different species.

claim: Condensin II is absent in some species including Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: In contrast, condensin II is absent in some species (e.g. fungi including Saccharomyces cerevisiae) or non-essential for mitosis in others (e.g. Drosophila melanogaster and Arabidopsis thaliana).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about condensin II distribution across species.

claim: Condensin II is non-essential for mitosis in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: In contrast, condensin II is absent in some species (e.g. fungi including Saccharomyces cerevisiae) or non-essential for mitosis in others (e.g. Drosophila melanogaster and Arabidopsis thaliana).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about condensin II function in different species.

claim: Condensin II is non-essential for mitosis in Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: In contrast, condensin II is absent in some species (e.g. fungi including Saccharomyces cerevisiae) or non-essential for mitosis in others (e.g. Drosophila melanogaster and Arabidopsis thaliana).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about condensin II function in different species.

claim: In Xenopus egg extracts, condensin I plays a dominant role in mitotic chromosome assembly.
source: In Xenopus egg extracts, condensin I plays a dominant role in mitotic chromosome assembly and condensin II makes a significant, yet rather minor contribution to this process (Choppakatla et al., 2021; Ono et al., 2003; Shintomi and Hirano, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies using Xenopus egg extracts.

claim: In Xenopus egg extracts, condensin II makes a significant, yet rather minor contribution to mitotic chromosome assembly.
source: In Xenopus egg extracts, condensin I plays a dominant role in mitotic chromosome assembly and condensin II makes a significant, yet rather minor contribution to this process (Choppakatla et al., 2021; Ono et al., 2003; Shintomi and Hirano, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies using Xenopus egg extracts.

claim: Condensin II has a specialized role in centromere assembly in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: Moreover, a specialized role of condensin II in centromere assembly has been reported in Xenopus egg extracts and in human cells (Barnhart-Dailey et al., 2017; Bernad et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Condensin II has a specialized role in centromere assembly in human cells.
source: Moreover, a specialized role of condensin II in centromere assembly has been reported in Xenopus egg extracts and in human cells (Barnhart-Dailey et al., 2017; Bernad et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Budding yeast condensin has the ability to translocate along a double-stranded DNA.
source: A recent breakthrough in the field was the demonstration that budding yeast condensin (classified as condensin I based on the primary structures of its subunits) has the ability to translocate along a double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) (Terakawa et al., 2017) and to 'extrude' a DNA loop (Ganji et al., 2018) in an ATP hydrolysis-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Budding yeast condensin has the ability to extrude a DNA loop in an ATP hydrolysis-dependent manner.
source: A recent breakthrough in the field was the demonstration that budding yeast condensin (classified as condensin I based on the primary structures of its subunits) has the ability to translocate along a double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) (Terakawa et al., 2017) and to 'extrude' a DNA loop (Ganji et al., 2018) in an ATP hydrolysis-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Human condensin I and condensin II display loop extrusion activities with slightly different properties in vitro.
source: Although it has been shown that human condensin I and condensin II display loop extrusion activities with slightly different properties in vitro (Kong et al., 2020), it remains unknown how such differences might be related to the different dynamics and functions of the two condensin complexes observed in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A recombinant condensin II holocomplex can functionally replace endogenous condensin II in Xenopus egg extracts lacking condensin I.
source: We find that a recombinant condensin II holocomplex can functionally replace endogenous condensin II in the extract lacking condensin I and enables the assembly of 'chenille-like' chromosomes with inner axes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from add-back assays shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Recombinant condensin II holocomplex enables the assembly of 'chenille-like' chromosomes with inner axes in Xenopus egg extracts lacking condensin I.
source: We find that a recombinant condensin II holocomplex can functionally replace endogenous condensin II in the extract lacking condensin I and enables the assembly of 'chenille-like' chromosomes with inner axes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and images shown in Figure 1.

claim: Recombinant condensin II holocomplex, when added at 200 nM, caused the formation of chromosomal structures similar to those formed by endogenous condensin II.
source: The addition of holo(WT) at 200 nM caused the formation of chromosomal structures similar to those formed by endogenous condensin II (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and images shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: The concentration of recombinant condensin II (200 nM) used in the assay was higher than the concentration of endogenous condensin II (~25 nM) in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: We noticed that this concentration (200 nM) was higher than the concentration of endogenous condensin II (~25 nM) in Xenopus egg extracts that had been estimated by proteomic analysis (Wühr et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with published proteomic data.

claim: ΔD3(WT) displayed a weak association with chromatin and failed to form DAPI-dense internal axes.
source: Unlike holo(WT), ΔD3(WT) displayed a weak association with chromatin and failed to form DAPI-dense internal axes (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: ΔG2(WT) retained the ability to assemble structures reminiscent of chenille-like chromosomes formed by holo(WT).
source: In contrast, ΔG2(WT) retained the ability to assemble structures reminiscent of chenille-like chromosomes formed by holo(WT) (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: An extremely high level of hCAP-H2 signals accumulated on DAPI-dense axes when ΔG2(WT) was used.
source: Strikingly, we noticed that an extremely high level of hCAP-H2 signals accumulated on DAPI-dense axes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: ΔG2(WT) became detectable on chromatin and initiated the formation of axes at much earlier time points than holo(WT).
source: A time-course of the formation of these chromosomes demonstrated that ΔG2(WT) became detectable on chromatin and initiated the formation of axes at much earlier time points than holo(WT) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ΔD3ΔG2(WT) displayed very little if any activity to associate with chromatin.
source: Unlike ΔG2(WT), ΔD3ΔG2(WT) displayed very little if any activity to associate with chromatin (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The addition of as low as 25 nM ΔG2(WT) was sufficient to produce chenille-like chromosomes similar to those formed by the addition of 200 nM holo(WT).
source: We found that the addition of as low as 25 nM ΔG2(WT) was sufficient to produce chenille-like chromosomes similar to those formed by the addition of 200 nM holo(WT) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: CAP-D3 has a positive role in chromosome association of condensin II that leads to chromosome axis formation.
source: These results suggest that CAP-D3 and CAP-G2 have a positive and negative role, respectively, in chromosome association of condensin II that leads to chromosome axis formation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing effects of CAP-D3 deletion.

claim: CAP-G2 has a negative role in chromosome association of condensin II that leads to chromosome axis formation.
source: These results suggest that CAP-D3 and CAP-G2 have a positive and negative role, respectively, in chromosome association of condensin II that leads to chromosome axis formation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing effects of CAP-G2 deletion.

claim: Holo(SMC-TR), when added at 200 nM, bound only weakly to chromatin, leaving an amorphous cloud-like structure.
source: We found that holo(SMC-TR), when added at 200 nM, bound only weakly to chromatin, leaving an amorphous cloud-like structure (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Chromosome association of ΔG2(SMC-TR) was greatly reduced compared to that of ΔG2(WT) at 200 nM.
source: At the same concentration, chromosome association of ΔG2(SMC-TR) was greatly reduced compared to that of ΔG2(WT), but was seen at a much higher level than that of holo(WT).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: ΔG2(SMC-TR) failed to show any sign of chromosome assembly despite high level of chromosome association.
source: Despite the high level of chromosome association, ΔG2(SMC-TR) failed to show any sign of chromosome assembly much like holo(SMC-TR).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ATP hydrolysis facilitates the accumulation of condensin II at the chromosome axes in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: These results suggest that ATP hydrolysis facilitates the accumulation of condensin II at the chromosome axes in Xenopus egg extracts.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data with SMC-TR mutants.

claim: Holo(WT) contained a modest level of ATPase activity in the absence of DNA but was stimulated more than twofold when dsDNA was added.
source: Holo(WT) contained a modest level of ATPase activity in the absence of DNA but was stimulated more than twofold when dsDNA was added (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ATPase assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Deletion of CAP-G2 resulted in more than threefold increase in ATP hydrolysis compared to holo(WT) in the absence of dsDNA.
source: On the other hand, deletion of CAP-G2 resulted in more than threefold increase in ATP hydrolysis compared to holo(WT) in the absence of dsDNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ATPase assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The ATPase activity of ΔG2(WT) was barely stimulated by adding dsDNA.
source: Intriguingly, the ATPase activity of ΔG2(WT) was barely stimulated by adding dsDNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ATPase assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The introduction of SMC-TR mutations greatly reduced the ATPase activities of both the holocomplex and ΔG2 subcomplex.
source: The introduction of SMC-TR mutations greatly reduced the ATPase activities of both the holocomplex and ΔG2 subcomplex.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ATPase assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CAP-G2 negatively regulates the ATPase activity of condensin II.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrated that CAP-G2 negatively regulates the ATPase activity of condensin II as well as its ability to associate with chromosomes.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing increased ATPase activity upon CAP-G2 deletion.

claim: CAP-G2 negatively regulates condensin II's ability to associate with chromosomes.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrated that CAP-G2 negatively regulates the ATPase activity of condensin II as well as its ability to associate with chromosomes.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing increased chromosome association upon CAP-G2 deletion.

claim: Human CAP-D3 is a polypeptide with 1498 amino acids.
source: Human CAP-D3 is a polypeptide with 1498 amino acids, in which a HEAT-repeat-rich section is followed by a C-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR) of around 200 amino-acid long (Figure 4A; Ono et al., 2003; Yoshimura and Hirano, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The CAP-D3 C-terminal IDR contains as many as 11 Cdk1 consensus (S/TP) sites.
source: Notably, the C-terminal IDR domain, which we refer to as the C-tail in the current study, contains as many as 11 Cdk1 consensus (S/TP) sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mitosis-specific phosphorylation in the CAP-D3 C-tail regulates condensin II functions.
source: Previous studies reported that mitosis-specific phosphorylation in the CAP-D3 C-tail regulates condensin II functions (Abe et al., 2011; Bakhrebah et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The full-length CAP-D3 (D3-FL), but not the C-terminally truncated version of CAP-D3 (D3-dC), underwent progressive, electrophoretic mobility shifts when incubated in metaphase extracts.
source: When holo(WT) and holo(D3-dC) were incubated in metaphase extracts, the full-length CAP-D3 (D3-FL), but not the C-terminally truncated version of CAP-D3 (D3-dC), underwent progressive, electrophoretic mobility shifts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The deletion of the CAP-D3 C-tail removed most, if not all, of the mitosis-specific phosphorylation sites.
source: A pair of phosphospecific antibodies against pT1415 and pS1474 recognized shifted D3-FL, but not D3-dC, suggesting that the deletion of the CAP-D3 C-tail removed most, if not all, of the mitosis-specific phosphorylation sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using phospho-specific antibodies shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The ATPase activity of holo(D3-dC) was significantly higher than that of holo(WT) either in the presence or absence of dsDNA.
source: In the ATPase assay, we found that the ATPase activity of holo(D3-dC) was significantly higher than that of holo(WT) either in the presence or absence of dsDNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ATPase assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Higher levels of chromosome association were observed with holo(D3-dC) than with holo(WT) at all concentrations tested (25, 50, and 200 nM).
source: In the add-back assay, higher levels of chromosome association were observed with holo(D3-dC) than with holo(WT) at all concentrations tested (25, 50, and 200 nM; Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The chromosome structure formed by holo(D3-dC) at 200 nM was no longer chenille-like: DAPI signals were more confined toward the axis positive for hCAP-H2.
source: Remarkably, we noticed that the chromosome structure formed by holo(D3-dC) at 200 nM was no longer chenille-like: DAPI signals were more confined toward the axis positive for hCAP-H2 (Figure 4C, left, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), being compacted laterally into structures reminiscent of rod-shaped chromosomes produced by condensin I (Kinoshita et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: When the concentration of holo(D3-dC) was lowered to 50 nM, its chromosome association was reduced to a level similar to that of holo(WT) at 200 nM addition and formed similar chenille-like chromosomes.
source: However, when the concentration of holo(D3-dC) was lowered to 50 nM, its chromosome association was reduced to a level similar to that of holo(WT) at 200 nM addition and formed similar chenille-like chromosomes (Figure 4C, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The CAP-D3 C-tail negatively regulates condensin II-mediated chromosome assembly.
source: These results demonstrated that the CAP-D3 C-tail negatively regulates condensin II-mediated chromosome assembly, and further implicated that a high level of chromosome association of holo(D3-dC) supports the conversion from chenille-like to laterally compacted rod-like structures.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing effects of CAP-D3 C-tail deletion.

claim: A high level of chromosome association of holo(D3-dC) supports the conversion from chenille-like to laterally compacted rod-like structures.
source: These results demonstrated that the CAP-D3 C-tail negatively regulates condensin II-mediated chromosome assembly, and further implicated that a high level of chromosome association of holo(D3-dC) supports the conversion from chenille-like to laterally compacted rod-like structures.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing dose-dependent effects.

claim: Slightly higher levels of chromosome association were observed with ΔG2(D3-dC) than with ΔG2(WT).
source: We found that slightly higher levels of chromosome association were observed with ΔG2(D3-dC) than with ΔG2(WT) (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The chromosomes formed by ΔG2(D3-dC) were chenille-like rather than rod-like, even at the highest concentration of 200 nM.
source: Importantly, however, the chromosomes formed by ΔG2(D3-dC), unlike those formed by holo(D3-dC), were chenille-like rather than rod-like, even at the highest concentration of 200 nM (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: CAP-G2 has a rather cryptic role in chromosome shaping, which can only be uncovered when the holocomplex is overloaded on chromosomes by deleting the CAP-D3 C-tail.
source: These results showed that CAP-G2 has a rather cryptic role in chromosome shaping, which can only be uncovered when the holocomplex is overloaded on chromosomes by deleting the CAP-D3 C-tail.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing holo(D3-dC) and ΔG2(D3-dC).

claim: Two basic amino acid clusters (BC1 and BC2) conserved in the central region of Brn1/CAP-H form part of a unique DNA-binding subdomain ('safety belt').
source: A previous study using budding yeast condensin had reported that two basic amino acid clusters (BC1 and BC2) conserved in the central region of Brn1/CAP-H form part of a unique DNA-binding subdomain ('safety belt'; Kschonsak et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous structural study.

claim: BC1/2 mutations in human CAP-H caused hypomorphic defects in condensin I-mediated chromosome assembly in Xenopus egg extract.
source: It had also been shown that BC1/2 mutations (substitutions of all basic residues with aspartic acids) in human CAP-H caused hypomorphic defects in condensin I-mediated chromosome assembly in Xenopus egg extract (Kinoshita et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The BC1D or BC2D mutations caused partial defects in chromosome association of condensin II, resulting in the formation of discontinuous axes.
source: We found that the BC1D or BC2D mutations caused partial defects in chromosome association of condensin II, resulting in the formation of discontinuous axes (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Holo(H2-BC1/2D), a holocomplex harboring both BC1D and BC2D mutations, failed to associate with chromatin, leaving a cloud-like morphology.
source: In contrast, holo(H2-BC1/2D), a holocomplex harboring both BC1D and BC2D mutations, failed to associate with chromatin, leaving a cloud-like morphology.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The two sets of BC mutations caused synergistic defects in condensin II-mediated chromosome assembly.
source: Thus, the two sets of mutations caused synergistic defects in condensin II-mediated chromosome assembly.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing single and double mutants.

claim: Deletion of CAP-G2 from mutant complexes harboring BC1D, BC2D, or BC1/2D partially rescued their defects in chromosome association and axis formation.
source: Interestingly, deletion of CAP-G2 from these mutant complexes harboring BC1D, BC2D, or BC1/2D partially rescued their defects in chromosome association and axis formation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the BC1/2D mutations do not cause complete loss of condensin II functions when the negative regulation by CAP-G2 is eliminated.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The BC1/2D mutations do not cause complete loss of condensin II functions when the negative regulation by CAP-G2 is eliminated.
source: Interestingly, deletion of CAP-G2 from these mutant complexes harboring BC1D, BC2D, or BC1/2D partially rescued their defects in chromosome association and axis formation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the BC1/2D mutations do not cause complete loss of condensin II functions when the negative regulation by CAP-G2 is eliminated.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing partial rescue.

claim: Condensin II holo(WT) displayed a weak ATP-stimulated binding and caused compaction of the banana-shaped chromatin in an ATP-dependent manner.
source: We found that condensin II holo(WT) displayed a weak ATP-stimulated binding and caused compaction of the banana-shaped chromatin in an ATP-dependent manner (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the extract-free assay shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Neither ATP-stimulated binding nor ATP-dependent compaction was observed when the ATP-hydrolysis-deficient holo(SMC-TR) was added.
source: Neither ATP-stimulated binding nor ATP-dependent compaction was observed when the ATP-hydrolysis-deficient holo(SMC-TR) was added.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the extract-free assay shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: ΔD3(WT) and ΔD3ΔG2(WT) were barely detectable on the chromatin in either the absence or presence of ATP in the extract-free assay.
source: ΔD3(WT) and ΔD3ΔG2(WT) were barely detectable on the chromatin in either the absence or presence of ATP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the extract-free assay shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: ΔG2(WT) displayed much greater activities of both ATP-stimulated binding and ATP-dependent compaction than holo(WT) in the extract-free assay.
source: Strikingly, ΔG2(WT) displayed much greater activities of both ATP-stimulated binding and ATP-dependent compaction than holo(WT).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the extract-free assay shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: The CAP-D3 C-tail lacking holo(D3-dC) displayed higher activities than holo(WT) in the extract-free assay.
source: The CAP-D3 C-tail lacking holo(D3-dC) was also tested and was found to display higher activities than holo(WT) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the extract-free assay shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The swollen chromatin binding assay allows probing for ATP-stimulated chromatin binding and ATP-dependent chromatin compaction by condensin II under an extract-free condition.
source: Thus, the swollen chromatin binding assay allows us to probe for ATP-stimulated chromatin binding and ATP-dependent chromatin compaction by condensin II under an extract-free condition.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results of the extract-free assay.

claim: The simple extract-free assay could recapitulate, at least in part, the differences in chromatin binding between the wild-type and the mutant complexes observed in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: Importantly, this simple assay could recapitulate, at least in part, the differences in chromatin binding between the wild-type and the mutant complexes observed in Xenopus egg extracts.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of results from extract-based and extract-free assays.

claim: In condensin I, the two HEAT subunits, CAP-D2 and CAP-G, have antagonistic functions in the dynamic assembly of chromosome axes.
source: A previous study from our laboratory had demonstrated that a pair of HEAT subunits of condensin I, CAP-D2, and CAP-G, have antagonistic functions in the dynamic assembly of chromosome axes (Kinoshita et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Deletion of CAP-G decreased chromosome association of condensin I and caused the formation of a chromosome structure with fuzzy surfaces and abnormally thin axes.
source: Deletion of CAP-G decreased chromosome association of condensin I and caused the formation of a chromosome structure with fuzzy surfaces and abnormally thin axes.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge from previous studies on condensin I.

claim: The essential requirement of CAP-D3 in condensin II-mediated axis formation was parallel to the requirements of CAP-D2 in condensin I-mediated axis formation.
source: Although the essential requirement of CAP-D3 in condensin II-mediated axis formation was parallel to the requirements of CAP-D2 in condensin I-mediated axis formation (Kinoshita et al., 2015; Kinoshita et al., 2022), we were surprised to find that CAP-G2 has a very strong negative impact on condensin II functions.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with previous studies on condensin I.

claim: The balancing acts of the two HEAT subunits, originally proposed for condensin I, also operate in condensin II, but such actions are fine-tuned differently in each complex.
source: We suggest that the balancing acts of the two HEAT subunits, originally proposed for condensin I (Kinoshita et al., 2015), also operate in condensin II, but that such actions are fine-tuned differently in each complex (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing condensins I and II.

claim: In condensin II, CAP-D3-driven axis assembly is intrinsically dominant, which is counter-balanced by the strong suppressive action of CAP-G2.
source: In the case of condensin II, for example, CAP-D3-driven axis assembly is intrinsically dominant, which is counter-balanced by the strong suppressive action of CAP-G2.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data on condensin II.

claim: Deletion of the CAP-D3 C-tail from the condensin I holocomplex causes no noticeable impact on mitotic chromosome assembly in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: This mode of regulation is unique to condensin II, because deletion of the CAP-D2 C-tail from the condensin I holocomplex causes no noticeable impact on mitotic chromosome assembly in Xenopus egg extracts (Figure 4—figure supplement 3; Kinoshita et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and citation.

claim: Deletion of the CAP-D3 C-tail has a greater impact on the holocomplex than on the ΔG2 subcomplex.
source: The observation that deletion of the CAP-D3 C-tail has a greater impact on the holocomplex than on the ΔG2 subcomplex (Figure 4) suggests an overlap in the negative regulatory roles of CAP-G2 and the CAP-D3 C-tail (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: There is an overlap in the negative regulatory roles of CAP-G2 and the CAP-D3 C-tail.
source: The observation that deletion of the CAP-D3 C-tail has a greater impact on the holocomplex than on the ΔG2 subcomplex (Figure 4) suggests an overlap in the negative regulatory roles of CAP-G2 and the CAP-D3 C-tail (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing effects of deletions.

claim: A recent study using cross-linking mass spectrometry has revealed physical contacts between an N-terminal region of CAP-G2 and a C-terminal region of CAP-D3.
source: A recent study using cross-linking mass spectrometry has revealed physical contacts between an N-terminal region of CAP-G2 and a C-terminal region of CAP-D3 (Kong et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: CAP-G2 may interfere with the action of CAP-D3 by directly interacting with the CAP-D3 C-tail.
source: It is therefore possible that CAP-G2 interferes with the action of CAP-D3 by directly interacting with the CAP-D3 C-tail.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from structural data.

claim: Mitosis-specific phosphorylation by Cdk1 of the CAP-D3 C-tail may destabilize the suppressing interaction with CAP-G2, thereby activating CAP-D3-mediated axis assembly.
source: Future experiments should test the hypothesis that mitosis-specific phosphorylation by Cdk1 of the CAP-D3 C-tail destabilizes the suppressing interaction, thereby activating CAP-D3-mediated axis assembly.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a hypothesis for future testing.

claim: The chromosome structure produced in Xenopus egg extract by holo(D3-dC) is qualitatively different from that produced by ΔG2(WT) and ΔG2(D3-dC).
source: Despite the potential functional crosstalk between CAP-G2 and the CAP-D3 C-tail, it is important to note that the chromosome structure produced in Xenopus egg extract by holo(D3-dC) is qualitatively different from that produced by ΔG2(WT) and ΔG2(D3-dC).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing chromosome morphologies.

claim: ΔG2(WT) and ΔG2(D3-dC) accumulate at the axis of chromosomes in a dose-dependent manner, but such accumulation does not cause enrichment of DNA at the axis.
source: While ΔG2(WT) and ΔG2(D3-dC) accumulate at the axis of chromosomes in a dose-dependent manner, such accumulation does not cause enrichment of DNA at the axis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: ΔG2(WT) and ΔG2(D3-dC) shift the chromosomal DNA to elongate the overall axis while keeping their chenille-like morphology under high-dose conditions.
source: Instead, ΔG2(WT) and ΔG2(D3-dC) shift the chromosomal DNA to elongate the overall axis while keeping their chenille-like morphology under high-dose conditions (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and illustrated in Figure 7B.

claim: Holo(D3-dC) increases the DNA level at the axial region under a high-dose condition and produces rod-like chromosomes rather than chenille-like chromosomes.
source: In contrast, holo(D3-dC) increases the DNA level at the axial region under a high-dose condition and produces rod-like chromosomes rather than chenille-like chromosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: CAP-G2 is not a mere inhibitor but has a rather cryptic function in the compaction of non-axial bulk chromatin.
source: These observations suggest that CAP-G2 is not a mere inhibitor but has a rather cryptic function in the compaction of non-axial bulk chromatin (Figure 7A, right).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing different mutants.

claim: The function of CAP-G2 in bulk chromatin compaction is observed only when the holocomplex is overloaded on chromosomes by deleting the CAP-D3 C-tail.
source: However, this function of CAP-G2 is observed only when the holocomplex is overloaded on chromosomes by deleting the CAP-D3 C-tail.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claim: Holo(D3-dC), but not ΔG2(WT), retains DNA-stimulated ATPase activity.
source: Intriguingly, we find that holo(D3-dC), but not ΔG2(WT), retains DNA-stimulated ATPase activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ATPase assays.

claim: ATP binding and hydrolysis by the SMC subunits are essential for the functions of condensin I in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: Our previous work demonstrated that ATP binding and hydrolysis by the SMC subunits are essential for the functions of condensin I in Xenopus egg extracts (Kinoshita et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The SMC ATPase cycle is essential for the functions of condensin II.
source: Thus, the SMC ATPase cycle is essential for the functions of condensin II, too, even in the absence of its inhibitory subunit CAP-G2.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data with SMC-TR mutants.

claim: Two basic patches (BC1 and BC2) present in the central region of budding yeast Brn1/CAP-H, together with Ycg1/CAP-G, have been proposed to form a unique DNA-binding region, referred to as the 'safety belt'.
source: Two basic patches (BC1 and BC2) present in the central region of budding yeast Brn1/CAP-H, together with Ycg1/CAP-G, have been proposed to form a unique DNA-binding region, referred to as the 'safety belt' (Kschonsak et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous structural study.

claim: The BC1/2D mutations in the CAP-H2 subunit of mammalian condensin II completely abolish its ability to associate with chromatin.
source: In contrast, our current results show that the BC1/2D mutations in the CAP-H2 subunit of mammalian condensin II completely abolish its ability to associate with chromatin (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: There has been no direct evidence to date that mammalian condensins use a safety-belt mechanism for DNA binding as demonstrated by budding yeast condensin.
source: Although the phenotypic differences observed between condensins I and II are intriguing, it should be noted that there has been no direct evidence to date that mammalian condensins use a safety-belt mechanism for DNA binding as demonstrated by budding yeast condensin.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the current state of the field.

claim: The functional requirement for CAP-G2 may be somewhat relaxed in condensin from the filamentous fungus Chaetomium thermophilum.
source: Even if a similar mechanism operates in mammalian condensin II, it is possible that the functional requirement for CAP-G2 is somewhat relaxed, as has been recently shown in condensin from the filamentous fungus Chaetomium thermophilum (Shaltiel et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: ΔG2(H2-BC1/2D), but not holo(H2-BC1/2D), retains the ability to associate with chromatin.
source: Moreover, it is worthy to note that ΔG2(H2-BC1/2D), but not holo(H2-BC1/2D), retains the ability to associate with chromatin, suggesting the existence of a loading pathway that is actualized in the absence of CAP-G2 (e.g. CAP-D3-dependent pathway).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: There may exist a loading pathway that is actualized in the absence of CAP-G2 (e.g. CAP-D3-dependent pathway).
source: Moreover, it is worthy to note that ΔG2(H2-BC1/2D), but not holo(H2-BC1/2D), retains the ability to associate with chromatin, suggesting the existence of a loading pathway that is actualized in the absence of CAP-G2 (e.g. CAP-D3-dependent pathway).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from experimental data.

claim: The formation of consecutive loops through a mechanism of loop extrusion has been proposed to underlie mitotic chromosome assembly.
source: It has been proposed that the formation of consecutive loops through a mechanism of loop extrusion underlies mitotic chromosome assembly (Goloborodko et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous modeling study.

claim: Condensin I is equipped with a loop extrusion-independent mechanism that contributes to mitotic chromosome assembly and shaping in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: In fact, a recent study from our laboratory has provided evidence that condensin I is equipped with a loop extrusion-independent mechanism that contributes to mitotic chromosome assembly and shaping in Xenopus egg extracts (Kinoshita et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The gap that currently exists between the nanoscale single-molecule assays and the mesoscale chromosome assembly assays needs to be filled.
source: The gap that currently exists between the nanoscale single-molecule assays and the mesoscale chromosome assembly assays needs to be filled (Birnie and Dekker, 2021).
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of current challenges in the field.

claim: The extract-free assay allowed recapitulation of ATP-stimulated chromatin binding of condensin II, which in turn results in compaction of the chromatin mass.
source: This simple assay allowed us to recapitulate ATP-stimulated chromatin binding of condensin II, which in turn results in compaction of the chromatin mass.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the extract-free assay.

claim: The current study has important implications for the evolution of condensin complexes.
source: The current study has important implications for the evolution of condensin complexes.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Condensin II subunits are not present in fungi including S. cerevisiae.
source: For instance, condensin II subunits are not present in fungi including S. cerevisiae.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about condensin evolution.

claim: The plant A. thaliana and the primitive alga Cyanidioschyzon merolae possess all three non-SMC subunits of condensin II, but they are non-essential for chromosome assembly and segregation in mitosis.
source: The plant A. thaliana and the primitive alga Cyanidioschyzon merolae possess all three non-SMC subunits of condensin II, but they are non-essential for chromosome assembly and segregation in mitosis (Fujiwara et al., 2013; Sakamoto et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The cap-g2 gene is missing in the genome of the fruit fly D. melanogaster.
source: Intriguingly, the cap-g2 gene is missing in the genome of the fruit fly D. melanogaster (Herzog et al., 2013), although the cap-d3 and cap-h2 genes have meiotic functions and participate in interphase chromosome territory formation (Hartl et al., 2008; Rosin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The cap-d3 and cap-h2 genes have meiotic functions and participate in interphase chromosome territory formation in D. melanogaster.
source: Intriguingly, the cap-g2 gene is missing in the genome of the fruit fly D. melanogaster (Herzog et al., 2013), although the cap-d3 and cap-h2 genes have meiotic functions and participate in interphase chromosome territory formation (Hartl et al., 2008; Rosin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Among the genes encoding the non-SMC subunits of condensin II, cap-g2 has been lost most frequently during insect evolution.
source: Moreover, a recent survey has revealed recurrent losses and rapid evolution of the condensin II complex in insect species (King et al., 2019): among the genes encoding the non-SMC subunits of condensin II, cap-g2 has been lost most frequently during insect evolution.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent evolutionary study.

claim: Condensin II can fulfill its functions largely, if not completely, even without the CAP-G2 subunit.
source: Thus, condensin II can fulfill its functions largely, if not completely, even without the CAP-G2 subunit, providing a possible explanation of why the cap-g2 gene tends to be lost during evolution in some species.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data and evolutionary observations.

claim: Condensin II acts as a determinant of chromosome architectures, namely, Rabl-like or territory-like configuration.
source: A recent three-dimensional genomics approach, which applies comprehensive Hi-C analyses to a wide variety of eukaryotic species, has reported that condensin II acts as a determinant of chromosome architectures, namely, Rabl-like or territory-like configuration (Hoencamp et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent Hi-C study.

claim: The functional contribution of condensin II was observed more prominently when mouse sperm nuclei were used as a substrate than when Xenopus sperm nuclei were used.
source: It was noticed that the functional contribution of condensin II was observed more prominently when mouse sperm nuclei were used as a substrate than when Xenopus sperm nuclei were used (Shintomi et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The slow kinetics of nucleosome assembly on the mouse sperm substrate creates an environment in favor of condensin II's action.
source: We suspected that the slow kinetics of nucleosome assembly on the mouse sperm substrate creates an environment in favor of condensin II's action.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from observations.

claim: Control extract (Δmock) produced a cluster of rod-shaped chromosomes.
source: As reported in a previous study (Shintomi et al., 2017), control extract (Δmock) produced a cluster of rod-shaped chromosomes whereas condensin I-depleted extract (Δcond I) produced a cluster of thick chromosomes with fuzzy surfaces in which condensin II localized to DAPI-dense axes (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C and citation.

claim: Condensin I-depleted extract (Δcond I) produced a cluster of thick chromosomes with fuzzy surfaces in which condensin II localized to DAPI-dense axes.
source: As reported in a previous study (Shintomi et al., 2017), control extract (Δmock) produced a cluster of rod-shaped chromosomes whereas condensin I-depleted extract (Δcond I) produced a cluster of thick chromosomes with fuzzy surfaces in which condensin II localized to DAPI-dense axes (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C and citation.

claim: Immunodepletion of both condensins I and II (Δcond I/II) resulted in the formation of an amorphous mass of chromatin (called 'cloud') in which twenty chromosomal DNAs are entangled with each other.
source: Immunodepletion of both condensins I and II (Δcond I/II) resulted in the formation of an amorphous mass of chromatin (called 'cloud') in which twenty chromosomal DNAs are entangled with each other.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Recombinant condensin II holocomplex, when added back into the Δcond I/II extract, effectively restored the ability to support condensin II-mediated chromosome assembly in a dose-dependent manner.
source: We found that recombinant condensin II holocomplex, when added back into the Δcond I/II extract, effectively restored the ability to support condensin II-mediated chromosome assembly in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Comparable levels of hCAP-H2 signals were detectable on the axes between 25 nM ΔG2(WT) and 200 nM holo(WT) conditions.
source: Comparable levels of hCAP-H2 signals were detectable on the axes between the two conditions (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A fraction of hCAP-H2 is phosphorylated when expressed in insect cells.
source: Phosphatase treatment of a purified sample, as described in the Dephosphorylation Assay subsection, caused one of the two bands positive for anti-hCAP-H2 to migrate faster (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), showing that a fraction of hCAP-H2 is phosphorylated in the host insect cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.
